The Craft of Extraction

By Jane Doe · March 14, 2026

Every reading pipeline lives or dies on one unglamorous step: turning a web page, with its navigation bars, cookie banners, newsletter upsells, and comment threads, into the clean text a person actually read. Get this wrong and everything downstream rots. Summaries summarize chrome, search indexes match footer boilerplate, and the archive you promised yourself becomes a junk drawer of markup.

The temptation is to treat extraction as a solved problem, something you bolt on in an afternoon with whatever library is nearest. In practice it is a long tail of small decisions, each one boring on its own, each one compounding. Which container holds the article? Is that pull quote content or decoration? Does the code sample survive the trip, or does it come out as a single mangled line with its indentation stripped and its angle brackets escaped?

Why boilerplate wins by default

A modern article page is mostly not the article. Measured by markup weight, the story is a minority tenant in its own house, surrounded by sharing widgets, related-content carousels, and three different subscription prompts. Any naive text dump inherits all of it. The classic answer is readability-style content scoring, the approach behind Readability, which walks the DOM, scores candidate blocks by text density, link density, and paragraph structure, and keeps the winner.

Scoring works because articles have a shape. Long paragraphs, real sentences with commas, few links per word. Chrome has the opposite shape: short strings, dense links, shallow nesting repeated across every page of the site. The algorithm does not need to understand the words to tell the difference, and that indifference is what makes it robust across a decade of redesigns.

The reader does not care how clever the pipeline is. The reader cares that the words on the page are the words the author wrote, all of them, in order, with nothing bolted on.

What must survive the trip

Extraction is a lossy transformation by design, but the losses have to be the right ones. Headings must survive, because they carry the skeleton of the argument. Links must survive, because a link is a citation and stripping it is a small act of vandalism. Blockquotes must survive, because attribution matters. And code must survive verbatim, fenced and intact, because a reader who saved a technical post wants the exact incantation, not a prose description of it. 

const captures = await drain(inbox);
for (const capture of captures) {
  persist(capture); // durable before any fetch is attempted
}

Everything else can go. Bylines are metadata, not body. Publication dates belong in frontmatter. The author photo, the estimated reading time, the floating share rail: none of it was ever part of the text. A good extractor is judged as much by what it refuses to keep as by what it keeps.

The honest failure matters most of all. When a page is a paywall shell or an empty JavaScript husk, the right output is a recorded failure that says so, queryable and retryable, never a confident summary of nothing. An archive you cannot trust to admit its gaps is worse than no archive, because it teaches you to stop checking.
